extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and readers interested in literary theory, dramatic theory, and Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and analysing classical tragedy as set out in Aristotle's Poetics: definition of tragedy, its parts (plot, character, thought, diction, melody, spectacle), and related devices (catharsis, hamartia, anagnorisis, peripeteia, unity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is a representation of a serious, complete action that has magnitude, in embellished speech, with each of its elements used separately in the parts and represented by people acting and not by narration, accomplished using pity and terror effecting the proper catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key components: seriousness, completeness, magnitude; embellished speech (rhythm and melody/song); enactment (action rather than narration); emotional aim is to produce pity and fear and to effect catharsis. The definition functions as a checklist: if a work lacks these features it is not a proper tragedy according to Aristotle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization of incidents; the plot should imitate an action that evokes pity and fear and be a change of fortune (from good to bad or vice versa). Complex plots include peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition); suffering and violent situations (especially between friends/family) evoke tragic emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots should be unified, driven by necessity and probability: actions must follow logically from preceding events and character. The most tragic plots typically push a good character toward undeserved misfortune because of a mistake (hamartia). Aristotle prefers plots where a threat is almost carried out in ignorance and then discovered at the last moment, although he discusses variants. Avoid loose, episodic plotting (epic-style plurality of actions) which dilutes tragic concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters reveal moral qualities through actions and choices; successful tragedy excites pity and fear by representing agents whose character supports the plot and whose motivations connect cause-and-effect chains producing those emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main character should be 'good' (not morally extreme), appropriate to their role (e.g., age and wisdom align), and internally consistent (actions follow probability and necessity). Sudden unexplained changes are anti-patterns — if a character shifts behavior, the cause should be shown. Characters should support and arise from the plot rather than merely serving incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (tragic error / miscalculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake or error (hamartia) by which a character brings about misfortune; in tragic plots it often explains undeserved suffering for a basically good person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hamartia to generate pity/fear by showing how error leads plausibly to catastrophe. Avoid making the protagonist villainous or wholly blameworthy, since that undermines the elicitation of pity. Hamartia should be integrated with character motives and the causal chain of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery or recognition within the plot that alters the situation (identification, revelation of facts about identity or circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anagnorisis paired with peripeteia (reversal) is especially powerful: recognition that precipitates or clarifies a reversal heightens tragic impact. The recognition should occur within the plot (not offstage) and feel necessary and probable given earlier events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversal of the situation, where the action veers round to its opposite, contributing to tragic emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best used in complex plots with linked anagnorisis; reversals should arise plausibly from prior events and character, not as arbitrary twists. Ideally the reversal yields greater tragic effect when combined with recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasoning, themes, or argued content expressed by characters — the spoken thought that conveys motivations, explanations, and thematic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought should be expressed through characters' speeches and actions, explaining motivations and clarifying the chain of causes. It helps the audience understand why events occur and binds theme to plot; avoid leaving crucial reasoning implicit or offstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality and appropriateness of speech and language in tragedy; speeches should reflect character and express meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction must match moral qualities and social standing of speakers and should make the thought intelligible and effective. Poetic ornament (rhythm, figures) belongs here. Poor or mismatched speech undermines character credibility and thematic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody / Chorus (melos & chorus as actor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (and chorus-as-music/dance) is an element of tragic composition; the chorus should act as one of the actors and take part in the action, contributing to the unity and pleasure of the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats melos as music-dance integral to Greek tragedy (chorus singing/dancing). The chorus should be woven into the plot, not a detached spectacle; it can contribute to emotional effect and unity. Consider music/dance when structuring scenes where chorus appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The visual apparatus of the play — sets, costumes, props, and visual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle regards spectacle as the least artistic element and least connected to the poet's craft; good spectacle can enhance but not substitute for strong plot, character, and diction. Anti-pattern: beautiful visuals cannot redeem bad acting or a weak story; spectacle should support, not compensate for, poetic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis / tragic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The emotional effect of tragedy: the arousal and proper purgation (catharsis) of pity and fear, producing tragic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy's success is measured by its capacity to provoke pity and fear and to bring about a catharsis; structure plot and character to guide audience emotions toward that purgation. Avoid gratuitous violence or sensationalism that arouses shock without meaningful pity/fear tied to the plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, completeness, and magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be a complete (whole) action with a certain magnitude and unity — its incidents form a single, coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic or fragmentary narratives; the plot should have a beginning, middle, and end with unity of action. Tragedy is superior to epic in concentration and unity; prefer a tightly focused action over a plurality of loosely related episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre distinctions (matter, subjects, method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes poetic genres by matter (language, rhythm, melody), subjects/agents (serious/virtuous for tragedy vs less virtuous for comedy), and method of imitation (narration vs direct speech/actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate medium and agent types: tragedy uses actors and direct speech and deals with noble or serious people; comedy deals with foibles of lesser people. Consider whether to mix elements (e.g., epic with song) and how that affects mimetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection of agents (tripartite division)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents/characters should be chosen relative to the audience: superior (better than audience), inferior (worse), or equal (same level); this affects the nature of imitation and audience response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select character types that fit the intended emotional and moral effects. A tragic protagonist usually occupies a position that makes their fall or suffering meaningful to the audience; mismatched social/ethical status can diminish credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of imitation (narration vs enactment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic forms differ by whether they use a narrator, direct speech, or actors speaking lines; tragedy typically uses direct enactment rather than narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For drama aim to present actions through actors onstage rather than summarizing events; enactment produces stronger emotional engagement. Mixed methods (partial narration) are possible (e.g., Homeric epic) but change the mimetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's craft: visualization, complication, and dénouement
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should visualize all scenes when creating the plot, incorporate complication and dénouement, and combine the elements of tragedy so the whole is cohesive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, mentally stage each scene for causal clarity and unity; ensure complications lead naturally to denouement and that elements (plot, character, diction, melody, spectacle) are integrated. Anti-pattern: treating scenes as interchangeable vignettes rather than parts of a causal whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs history: necessity and universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (tragedy) deals with what might occur — determined by necessity and probability and unified by plot — whereas history deals with particular past events subject to contingency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating poetic narratives, value the way plot reveals general truths or universals via necessary/probable causal chains; don't expect historical exactness. A good poetic plot conveys philosophical insight about human action by showing plausible necessity.
